extracted.intended_audience: bankruptcy practitioners, judges, litigators, trustees, creditors, law students, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Supreme Court statutory interpretation of 11 U.S.C. §1123(b)(6) and related Bankruptcy Code provisions addressing whether and when a Chapter 11 plan may release or enjoin claims against nondebtors without affected claimants' consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ejusdem_generis application to §1123(b)(6)
rubrics_metrics.description: When faced with a catchall phrase like paragraph (6), courts interpret it in light of its surrounding context and read it to 'embrace only objects similar in nature' to the specific examples preceding it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paragraph (6) follows five specific paragraphs that 'all concern the debtor’s rights and responsibilities, as well as its relationship with its creditors.' Thus the catchall in §1123(b)(6) must be read to permit only additional plan provisions similar to those listed in paragraphs (1)–(5), not to confer radically different powers (Epic Systems Corp. v. Lewis; McBoyle example). The phrase 'any other appropriate provision' is context-dependent and draws meaning from surrounding provisions; it does not mean 'everything not expressly prohibited is permitted.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonconsensual nondebtor discharge not authorized
rubrics_metrics.description: The bankruptcy code does not authorize a release and injunction that, as part of a plan of reorganization under Chapter 11, effectively seeks to discharge claims against a nondebtor without the consent of affected claimants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A plan provision that would extinguish claims against third parties (here, the Sacklers) without claimants' consent cannot be grounded in §1123(b)(6) because that provision must be read in the context of debtor-focused paragraphs (1)–(5). The Court confined its holding to this question and did not disturb consensual third-party releases or plans providing full satisfaction of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discharge reserved to debtor who places assets on the table
rubrics_metrics.description: The code generally reserves discharge for a debtor who places substantially all of their assets on the table (see §§1141(d)(1)(A), 541(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordinarily, a Chapter 11 discharge requires the debtor to come forward with virtually all assets for distribution to creditors; a nondebtor who has not filed for bankruptcy and not placed virtually all assets on the table cannot obtain the discharge's benefits through a reorganization plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory limits on discharge (fraud, willful/malicious injury, jury rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: The discharge does not include claims based on 'fraud' or those alleging 'willful and malicious injury' (§§523(a)(2), (4), (6)), and it cannot affect a creditor’s right to jury trial for personal injury or wrongful death (28 U.S.C. §1411(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan proponents cannot evade these statutory limitations by rebranding discharges as 'releases.' A plan that purports to extinguish fraud or willful injury claims against nondebtors without consent transgresses explicit Code limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: §105(a) cannot be used to create authority not conferred elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 105(a) allows bankruptcy courts to 'issue any order, process, or judgment that is necessary or appropriate to carry out the provisions of' the bankruptcy code, but it cannot be used alone to justify nonconsensual third-party releases because it serves only to carry out authorities expressly conferred elsewhere in the Code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan proponents who invoke §105(a) must identify some express Code authority that §105(a) is carrying out; §105(a) is not a freestanding grant of power to create nonconsensual releases of third parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between derivative/estate claims and victims' direct claims
rubrics_metrics.description: A bankruptcy plan may settle or adjust claims or interests 'belonging to the debtor or to the estate' (§1123(b)(3)), including derivative claims that substantively belong to the debtor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolving derivative claims (claims that belong to the estate) is permissible under the listed paragraphs; but extinguishing claims that belong substantively to third-party victims (claims against nondebtors) is categorically different and not authorized by §1123(b)(3) or the other debtor-focused provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that plan provisions be 'appropriate' and consistent with Code
rubrics_metrics.description: Paragraph (6) permits 'any other appropriate provision not inconsistent with the applicable provisions of this title.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The word 'appropriate' is context-dependent and must be read against the statutory scheme; any provision adopted under §1123(b)(6) must not be inconsistent with other applicable provisions of the Bankruptcy Code and should be similar in nature to the provisions listed in paragraphs (1)–(5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical practice informs ambiguous provisions but does not override text
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-Code and historical practice—through 1978 and earlier bankruptcy laws—generally reserved discharge to a debtor offering a 'fair and full surrender' of property; history may inform ambiguous provisions but cannot be used to override clear statutory text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Court relied on historical practice to reject an expansive reading of §1123(b)(6): had Congress intended to permit nonconsensual nondebtor discharges, it likely would have said so expressly somewhere in the Code (citing RadLAX, Dewsnup, Sturges v. Crowinshield). Historical practice supports limiting extraordinary discharge-like relief to debtors who surrender assets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrowness of decision — preservation of consensual releases and full satisfaction plans
rubrics_metrics.description: The decision is narrow: it does not call into question consensual third-party releases offered in connection with a bankruptcy reorganization plan, nor does it express a view on what qualifies as a consensual release or on plans that provide for full satisfaction of claims against a third-party nondebtor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts and plan proponents retain ability to craft consensual solutions and to negotiate settlements that fully satisfy claims; the opinion addresses only nonconsensual releases that effectively discharge nondebtors without affected claimants' consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of courts vs policy arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy reasons (e.g., that nonconsensual releases facilitate settlements and recovery for creditors/victims) cannot supplant the text and structure of the Bankruptcy Code; the Court's task is to interpret and apply the law, not to resolve policy tradeoffs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although collective-action problems and practical consequences (mass torts, asbestos, Boy Scouts, etc.) bear on policy, they do not authorize courts to read statutory catchalls more broadly than the text and structure permit; policy arguments may be for Congress to address.
